## Start with a familiar regression

<div class="section-kicker">Use formulas where they help</div>

:::: {.grid-2 .wide-left}
::: {.card .accent-blue}
```{.julia brm-example="gaussian"}
```
:::
::: {.card .accent-teal}
**The formula handles the regression.**

`mu ~ 1 + x` gives an intercept and a slope.

`effect(...)` assigns priors to those coefficients.

The noise parameter and observation distribution are written alongside them.
:::
::::

<div class="takeaway">The aim: keep this convenience when a model needs more than regression.</div>
<div class="source-note">Existing executable example from the <a href="https://github.com/nsiccha/BayesianRegressionModels.jl/blob/ns/devibe/docs/src/feature-atlas.md">feature atlas</a>. Julia setup: <code>using BayesianRegressionModels, Distributions</code>.</div>

::: {.notes}
The code is extracted during rendering from the Gaussian example in docs/src/feature-atlas.md, which the documentation build executes. It includes real data and coefficient priors. The first effect statement sets Normal(0,2) priors; the more specific statement assigns Normal(0,0.25) to the slope. Normal's second argument is a standard deviation. Start with what users write, before introducing implementation details.
:::

## Add the part that describes your science

<div class="section-kicker">Example: drug concentration in each subject</div>

:::: {.grid-2 .wide-left}
::: {.card .accent-teal .model-code}
```{.julia brm-example="population_pk" brm-part="body"}
```
:::
::: {.card .accent-blue .tight}
**Formula lines:** describe how clearance (`CL`) and volume (`V`) vary between subjects.

**Custom calculation:** the `do` block computes the concentration curve.

**Observation line:** compares that curve with measured concentrations.

The shared `pk` label allows clearance and volume effects to be correlated.
:::
::::

<div class="takeaway">Formulas and a custom calculation live in the same model declaration.</div>
<div class="source-note"><strong>StanBlocks example.</strong> Turing currently rejects this ragged response. Body of the existing <code>@brm begin … end</code> declaration; complete code and data in appendix B. <code>kernel</code> runs the calculation for each subject.</div>

::: {.notes}
This is the body of the exact population_pk declaration from docs/src/feature-atlas.md. The Lua filter extracts it rather than maintaining a second copy. The structural equation is a one-compartment IV-bolus model: C(t) = dose/V * exp(-(CL/V)t). The log link is explicit on CL and V. The do-block receives evaluated subject-level values. This demonstrates formula/custom-code composition without asserting that every Julia operation is supported by every backend.
:::

## Subjects and measurements can fit together

<div class="section-kicker">The same PK example</div>

:::: {.grid-2 .wide-left}
::: {.card .accent-blue .model-code}
```{.julia brm-example="population_pk" brm-part="data"}
```
:::
::: {.card .accent-teal}
**Two subjects, five measurements.**

Each subject has a dose, clearance, and volume. Each measurement has a time and a subject label.

`ragged(time, obs_subject)` groups the times for the calculation. The response uses the same grouping.
:::
::::

<div class="takeaway">Describe subject differences with formulas; evaluate the curve at each subject’s measurement times.</div>
<div class="source-note">Data fields passed to the declaration on the previous slide. The interleaved rows are intentional.</div>

::: {.notes}
The example has two subject rows and five observation rows. alice has three measurements and bob has two; the rows are interleaved. The public kernel/ragged terms join these structures. This is a concrete data-alignment example, not a claim that a data.frame interface prevents another package from expressing the model.
:::

## The same approach reaches larger models

<div class="section-kicker">Existing BRM examples with custom scientific calculations</div>

:::: {.grid-3}
::: {.card .accent-blue .tight}
**Warfarin PK/PD**

Subject effects feed concentration calculations and an ODE for drug response.

[Full equations, code, and audit](https://github.com/nsiccha/BayesianRegressionModels.jl/blob/ns/devibe/docs/src/warfarin.md)

<span class="status stan">StanBlocks</span>

<div class="small">Public two-stage model: compilation and finite density/gradient checks. A joint extension is documented separately.</div>
:::
::: {.card .accent-teal .tight}
**Wastewater**

Regression and group effects combine with infection renewal, shedding, and measurement models.

[Formula and calculation definitions](https://github.com/nsiccha/BayesianRegressionModels.jl/blob/ns/devibe/docs/src/wastewater-cdc.md)

<span class="status stan">StanBlocks</span>

<div class="small">Structural port: compilation and finite density/gradient checks; not a numerically equivalent CDC reproduction.</div>
:::
::: {.card .accent-violet .tight}
**Grey-seal population**

Covariate and group effects combine with a population process and eight observation streams.

[Formula and population-process code](https://github.com/nsiccha/BayesianRegressionModels.jl/blob/ns/devibe/docs/src/seal-brm.md)

<span class="status stan">StanBlocks</span>

<div class="small">Compilation checks on an example dataset; no completed posterior fit. Turing does not execute this structural model.</div>
:::
::::

<div class="takeaway">Keep the useful regression formulas as the scientific calculation becomes more involved.</div>

::: {.notes}
These are examples of model construction, with their actual verification levels shown. They are not three new sampling success claims. The interesting custom definitions and how the formulas use them are linked together in the executable documentation. Warfarin's two-stage source and BRM's joint variant must not be conflated. The CDC port preserves structural relationships but does not reproduce all upstream hyperpriors and switches. The seal declaration adds estimated group scales to some effects; it should not be described as statistically identical to every upstream parameterization.
:::

## Compare the same modeling task

<div class="section-kicker">Subject effects + a custom concentration curve</div>

<div class="comparison-row header"><div>Approach</div><div>Regression and subject effects</div><div>Custom scientific calculation</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>brms</strong></div><div>Formula-based regression and nonlinear parameter models.</div><div>Nonlinear expressions and custom Stan functions; custom families have additional prediction and likelihood hooks.</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>BRM</strong></div><div>Formula-based regression and subject effects inside the model block.</div><div>The PK example passes their values directly into a custom calculation, then uses its result in the likelihood.</div></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><div><strong>Hand-written Stan or Turing</strong></div><div>Write the coefficients, group distributions, and predictor calculations explicitly.</div><div>Write the scientific calculation in the modeling language and its supported libraries.</div></div>

<div class="takeaway">BRM’s attraction is the combination: concise regression code with room for the rest of the model.</div>
<div class="source-note"><a href="https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/articles/brms_nonlinear.html">brms nonlinear models</a> · <a href="https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/stanvar.html">custom Stan code</a> · <a href="https://turinglang.org/docs/tutorials/bayesian-differential-equations/">Turing with differential equations</a>. This compares authoring approaches, not measured development time or fitting speed.</div>

::: {.notes}
brms is a mature, extensible modeling package. custom_family and stanvar are supported interfaces, and its data.frame input is not evidence of a hard statistical limitation. Turing already composes Julia model code with differential-equation solvers. The comparison therefore concerns what BRM lets the user express concisely, not an exclusive ability to use custom functions or a quantitative implementation-cost advantage.
:::

## Custom code has specific requirements

<div class="section-kicker">Flexibility in practice</div>

:::: {.grid-2}
::: {.card .accent-blue}
**A Julia function or distribution**

Turing can call ordinary Julia code retained by BRM.

It still needs the operations used by the fit: a valid density, a supported gradient path, and sampling support when generating predictions.
:::
::: {.card .accent-teal}
**A custom Stan calculation**

StanBlocks needs code it can translate to Stan.

A function written only for that path needs a Julia implementation before Turing can use it.
:::
::::

<div class="takeaway">Adding a calculation and adding a reusable model term are different amounts of work.</div>
<div class="source-note">A new parameter structure or fitted transform may need extra methods. See <a href="https://github.com/nsiccha/BayesianRegressionModels.jl/blob/ns/devibe/docs/refactoring.md">the current extension contracts</a>.</div>

::: {.notes}
Prepared expressions retain callable objects. Ordinary deterministic functions and distributions generally need no BRM compiler changes. Distribution factories may need brm_distribution_type to declare their result shape; Stan execution also needs a complete-call translation. New parameter structures and fitted terms need explicit preparation and execution methods. Support for one operation does not establish support for every wrapper, prediction operation, or backend.
:::

## A different parameterization can help sampling

<div class="section-kicker">Same probability model, different variables for the sampler</div>

:::: {.grid-2}
::: {.equation-panel}
**Sample the coefficient directly**

$$
\beta_k \sim \mathcal N(0,s_k)
$$

Often useful when the data strongly identify the coefficient.
:::
::: {.equation-panel}
**Sample a scaled coefficient**

$$
z_k \sim \mathcal N(0,1), \qquad \beta_k=s_k z_k
$$

Often useful when the data provide less information.
:::
::::

<div class="takeaway">BRM’s HSGP example can choose between these forms separately for each coefficient.</div>
<div class="small muted">The example models motorcycle-impact acceleration over time, with a Gaussian process for the mean and another for the noise level. It uses all 133 observations and 20 basis functions per process.</div>

::: {.notes}
These are centered and noncentered parameterizations. Neither is universally better. The scale s_k can depend on sampled hyperparameters, so the choice affects posterior geometry. Stan's reparameterization guide and Papaspiliopoulos, Roberts, and Sköld (2007) describe the information-dependent tradeoff. The next slide shows this specific BRM study, not a general guarantee. Appendix D gives the partial-centering transform and exact source model.
:::

## One model, three recorded fits

<div class="section-kicker">Corrected HSGP study · StanBlocks sampling</div>

:::: {.grid-2 .wide-left .case-result-grid}
::: {.card .accent-violet .tight .case-result-figure}
<img src="../../src/assets/adaptive-hsgp/online_centeredness.png" alt="Centeredness for each of the 20 basis frequencies in the mean and log-noise Gaussian processes, comparing online warmup and offline pilot selection">

<div class="tiny muted">Each coefficient gets its own choice. Zero is fully noncentered; one is fully centered. The two selection procedures need not agree.</div>
:::
::: {.case-result-stack}
<div class="card accent-coral case-result"><span class="label demo">Noncentered pilot</span><strong>10,000 draws · 34 divergences</strong><span>max split R-hat 1.0012 · min bulk/tail ESS 2,514 / 2,886</span></div>
<div class="card accent-amber case-result"><span class="label demo">Fresh partially centered fit</span><strong>10,000 draws · 16 divergences</strong><span>max split R-hat 1.0007 · min bulk/tail ESS 2,533 / 1,797</span></div>
<div class="card accent-teal case-result"><span class="label demo">Separate online extension</span><strong>10,000 draws · 0 divergences</strong><span>max split R-hat 1.0018 · min bulk/tail ESS 2,318 / 2,775</span></div>
:::
::::

<div class="case-boundaries"><div><strong>One chain per fit.</strong> These counts do not establish a general improvement in speed or accuracy. Split R-hat compares parts of the same chain.</div><div><strong>No corrected Turing samples.</strong> Target-value agreement and warmed gradient runtime still need verification.</div></div>

::: {.notes}
Counts and diagnostics come from research/adaptive_centering/results/source-faithful/diagnostics.tsv and online_diagnostics.tsv. All fits retain 10,000 draws, use Xoshiro(1), and keep WarmupHMC defaults. The source reproduction is the pilot plus fresh selected-partial refit; the online run is a separate extension. Offline selection searches 0:0.01:1; online warmup uses 0:0.1:1. The partial refit's minimum tail ESS is lower than the pilot's. No runtime comparison or cross-model advantage is established. A divergence indicates a numerical sampling problem; zero observed divergences is not proof of an accurate posterior. Appendix E gives the verification boundary.
:::

## Make predictions with the fitted model

<div class="section-kicker">Keep the meaning of the regression when the data change</div>

:::: {.grid-3}
::: {.card .accent-blue}
**During fitting**

Store the category levels, scaling constants, spline knots, and GP basis used to construct the model.
:::
::: {.card .accent-teal}
**For new measurements**

Apply those same transformations to new inputs, so the posterior coefficients still have the same meaning.
:::
::: {.card .accent-amber}
**For new subjects**

Choose explicitly how new group effects are generated. Check that the model and execution path support the requested prediction.
:::
::::

<div class="takeaway">Custom model components should fit into the prediction workflow as well as the model declaration.</div>
<div class="source-note">Current operations have documented limits; this is not a claim that every custom component already supports every prediction task.</div>

::: {.notes}
BRM's reprocess and descriptor/operation APIs retain fitted preparation. Unknown levels and unsupported extrapolation report a diagnostic. New-group resampling is an explicit operation for supported group structures. Warfarin's audit records limits on exposing all requested output arrays in one compiled model. Keep that distinction visible instead of promising automatic replay for arbitrary code. Sources: docs/refactoring.md and docs/src/turing-backend.md.
:::

## A possible future: Julia models on GPUs

<div class="section-kicker">A concrete direction to investigate</div>

:::: {.grid-2}
::: {.card .accent-blue}
**The compiler path exists**

Reactant compiles Julia computations through MLIR and XLA for CPU, GPU, and TPU execution.

It also documents a probabilistic-programming interface, including custom log-density functions.
:::
::: {.card .accent-amber}
**BRM integration remains to be shown**

A possible next step is to compile suitable Julia model code through this path.

Compatibility, gradients, and useful performance need to be demonstrated on actual BRM models.
:::
::::

<div class="takeaway">Keep the model declaration useful as more of its computation can run on accelerators.</div>
<div class="source-note"><a href="https://enzymead.github.io/Reactant.jl/stable/">Reactant</a> · <a href="https://enzymead.github.io/Reactant.jl/stable/tutorials/probprog/">probabilistic programming</a> · <a href="https://enzymead.github.io/Reactant.jl/stable/tutorials/control-flow">control-flow requirements</a>. brms already exposes <a href="https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/opencl.html">Stan/OpenCL support for some operations</a>; GPU access alone is not the proposed distinction.</div>

::: {.notes}
This is a possible future BRM integration, not a delivered backend or a performance promise. Reactant's documented Julia-to-MLIR/XLA path supports accelerators, and Reactant.ProbProg offers generative and custom-log-density modes. A generated Turing model is not thereby proved Reactant-compatible. Traced arrays, supported operations, and control-flow handling matter. Broader compilation of suitable Julia model computations is the direction, rather than a claim that other packages cannot use GPUs. Primary documentation checked 2026-09-14; the README records the unresolved Wren attribution.
:::

## Simple formulas, room for custom models {.main-end}

<div class="section-kicker" style="color:#f5ead8;">End of main talk</div>

<div class="lede">Use concise formulas for the regression parts, and combine them with custom model code when the science needs more.</div>

<div class="rule"></div>

<div class="small" style="max-width:44em;">The PK example shows the idea today. The larger examples show where it can go—and which execution and prediction details still need work.</div>

::: {.notes}
The selling point is the authoring experience: retaining formula convenience within a larger scientific model. Execution choices are useful supporting capabilities, with current coverage in the appendix. Do not substitute a speculative inference-method agenda for this benefit. Prospective guests and cited authors have not reviewed or endorsed the deck.
:::

## The centering study in detail

<span class="appendix-badge">Appendix D</span>

:::: {.grid-2 .wide-right .case-study-grid}
::: {.card .accent-teal .tight .case-model}
**Mean and noise both vary with time**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu(t)&=\operatorname{HSGP}_{\mu}(t),\\
\log\sigma(t)&=\operatorname{HSGP}_{\sigma}(t),\\
y(t)&\sim\mathcal N(\mu(t),\sigma(t)).
\end{aligned}
$$

Each GP uses 20 basis functions. Its log length scale and log marginal standard deviation have $\mathcal N(0,4)$ priors.

**Partial centering**

$$
u_k\sim\mathcal N(0,s_k^{c_k}),\qquad
\beta_k=s_k^{1-c_k}u_k.
$$
:::
::: {.card .accent-violet .tight .case-source-figure}
<img src="../../src/assets/adaptive-hsgp/selected_centeredness.png" alt="Offline pilot selects one centeredness value for each of the 20 frequencies in both Gaussian processes">
<div class="case-flow"><span><b>1</b> noncentered pilot</span><span><b>2</b> choose each $c_k$</span><span><b>3</b> fresh partial fit</span></div>
:::
::::

<div class="case-invariant">The source reproduction has two fits. Online adaptation is a separate BRM extension.</div>

::: {.notes}
All 133 MASS::mcycle rows; acceleration divided by its sample standard deviation; time mapped to [-1,1]; sine basis on [-1.5,1.5], normalized by 1/sqrt(1.5); no population intercept. Normal(0,4) on each source log hyperparameter is represented by LogNormal(0,4) on its positive BRM parameter with the matching unconstraining Jacobian. Offline centeredness search: 0:0.01:1, 40 coefficients total. The source's centered scatter panels transform pilot draws; there is no centered sampling arm. HSGP reference: Riutort-Mayol et al. (2023). Full hashes and source links are in the README.
:::

## What the centering results establish

<span class="appendix-badge">Appendix E</span>

:::: {.grid-2}
::: {.card .accent-teal .tight}
**Recorded evidence**

- All 133 rows; 20 basis functions per GP.
- `Xoshiro(1)`; 10,000 retained draws per fit; unchanged WarmupHMC defaults.
- Original Stan density and gradient checks: 26 for the noncentered target; 51 for the partial target.
- All 40 offline choices match the source-literal calculation.
- Complete-record and figure verification: 8,221 checks.
:::
::: {.card .accent-amber .tight}
**Limits of the conclusion**

- One chain per fit; split R-hat is a within-chain diagnostic.
- Divergences: 34, 16, and 0 in these runs.
- The partial refit has lower minimum tail ESS than the pilot.
- No general speed or accuracy advantage is established.
- No corrected Turing samples exist.
:::
::::

<div class="source-note">Corrected case <code>ea27c18ed2517e3061f441971f561235f48cceb8</code>, integrated as <code>2db645e5e9bdc59465ecdaa18d039460f682cda2</code>. <a href="https://github.com/nsiccha/BayesianRegressionModels.jl/tree/ns/devibe/research/adaptive_centering/results/source-faithful">Committed diagnostics, provenance, and audits</a>.</div>

::: {.notes}
The partial target was compared with the original adaptive Stan program at 16 saved posterior positions; maximum absolute density/gradient differences were 1.14e-13/4.96e-12. The online run uses the same full model and sampler defaults with a 0:0.1:1 warmup grid. Turing model generation does not establish target agreement: the explicit length-scale prior retained a default lower bound, and its gradient path remained too slow. Matched target-value and warmed-runtime checks must pass before corrected Turing sampling. Old reduced-basis/reduced-draw smoke results are superseded.
:::
